bullets: How to share $48 in the ratio 2:3 by splitting the whole into 5 equal parts and finding one part first
slides.heading: Ratio: sharing $48 in 2:3
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we share money in a ratio - what 2:3 really means, and how to find each share - and by the end you will be able to explain why a share is never bigger than the whole.

bullets: Read a ratio as parts of one whole: 2:3 means 2 parts and 3 parts
Find the whole in parts first: 2 + 3 = 5 parts
Share $48 in 2:3 by finding one part, then multiplying: 1 part = $9.60
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A classmate says the 3-part share of $48 in the ratio 2:3 is 3/2 of $48, which is $72
Is that possible? Can one share be more than the whole $48?
slides.heading: Can one share be $72?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands: can a share of $48 be $72, or must something be wrong? Take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because scene s2 settles this exactly.

bullets: A ratio of 2:3 splits one whole into 2 parts for one person and 3 parts for another, and every part is the same size
The whole matters: here the whole is $48 split into 5 equal parts, so each share is a part of the $48
slides.heading: A ratio compares parts of one whole
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: a ratio counts equal parts of one whole, and the shares must add back up to the whole.

bullets: Two children share $48 in the ratio 2:3: 2 parts for child A and 3 parts for child B
Add the parts to find the whole: 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts
slides.heading: Sharing in a ratio
slides.notes: Point at the parts as they appear and narrate: A takes two parts, B takes three parts, and every part is the same size.

bullets: Careful - the trap is: A ratio of 3:2 means 3/2 of the whole.
The whole is 5 parts, so 3 parts is 3 out of 5 - 3/5 of the whole, not 3/2 of it
slides.heading: Watch out: 3:2 is not 3/2 of the whole
slides.notes: Hold the claim up against the bar: 3/2 of $48 would be $72, more than the whole itself, so it cannot be a share of $48.

bullets: Five equal parts share $48, so 1 part = $48 / 5 = $9.60
Multiply for each share: A gets 2 x $9.60 = $19.20 and B gets 3 x $9.60 = $28.80
slides.heading: One part, then multiply
slides.notes: Narrate the split slowly: divide for one part first, then multiply by the number of parts each child takes. The shares are $19.20 and $28.80.

bullets: To share in a ratio: add the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for each share
Check the answer: $19.20 + $28.80 = $48, the whole we started with
slides.heading: The takeaway
slides.notes: Land the whole chain in one breath: add for the whole in parts, divide for one part, multiply for each share - A gets $19.20 and B gets $28.80.

bullets: Work the share in three steps: add 2 + 3 = 5 parts, divide $48 / 5 = $9.60 for one part, then multiply for each share
slides.heading: Worked example: sharing $48 in 2:3
slides.notes: Talk through the three steps slowly as in scene s3 and name each one as you write it; say: finding one part first keeps the working honest.

bullets: Share $60 in the ratio 2:3. Use the same idea: find one part first
Careful - a classmate says the 3-part share is 3/2 of $60. Correct them in one sentence, naming what the whole in parts really is
slides.heading: Your turn: share in a ratio
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the one-part step first, then on the exact sentence they used to correct the claim.

bullets: On your own: share $48 in the ratio 2:3, showing the one-part step
Watch out for the trap one last time: say what fraction of the whole the 3-part share really is, and why
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the one-part step in your first answer, plus one clear sentence about the 5 parts in your second.
